# Sensing and Perception {#sensing}

Navigation is the problem of estimating where a system is, how it is moving, and how it is oriented relative to some reference. Perception is how the system gets evidence about those quantities from the physical world. In practice, the two are tightly coupled: our navigation state determines what a sensor should see, and sensor measurements tell us whether our navigation state is plausible. This part of the course focuses on that second direction: based on what we see, how plausible is our navigation state? We start here for several practical and pragmatic reasons.

A useful way to think about perception is as the inverse side of navigation. Navigation asks:

> Given my previous state and my motion inputs, where do I think I am now?

Perception asks:

> Given what I observe now, what does that tell me about where I am?

If one or the other side is perfect, we have no need for the other. If I have a perfect measurement that directly relates to where I think I am then I have no further need of any additional math. For example, consider a one-dimensional hallway that goes from left to right. I am precisely two meters to the left of the green door. The green door is located five meters from the start of the hallway, therefore I am three meters from the start of the hallway. I don't care how uncertain my movement is: I can move about this hallway with my eyes closed. All I need to do is periodically open my eyes and look at how far away I am from the green door.

The inverse problem is also true: if I have perfect knowledge of my motion (I walk around with my eyes open) I have no need of making measurements provided I know my precise starting location.

In practice however, neither side is perfect. A motion model accumulates error because the real world is not exactly described by our equations and because the inputs are noisy. A measurement model corrects that drift, but only when the measurement is correctly interpreted. A camera image, a lidar scan, a GPS fix, and an accelerometer sample are not "truth." They are data produced by physical instruments with bias, noise, limits, and failure modes.

A practical demonstration of this is to walk around your home with your eyes closed. You may not touch the wall and may only open your eyes if you stop moving. Most people have a decent mental map of their home as well as having a reasonable sense of their own relative motion (proprioception) but you'll quickly notice that you will get a bit lost the longer you walk about with your eyes closed!

It is useful to borrow two terms from biology to describe the two broad classes of sensing and perception:

- **Proprioception**: sensing internal motion, force, and body state.
- **Exteroception**: sensing the external world.

For navigation, proprioceptive sensors usually support propagation. Examples include IMUs, wheel encoders, joint encoders, airspeed sensors, and Doppler velocity logs. They tell the system how it is moving, but they usually do not directly tell it where it is relative to an external map. We group these sensor readings as the "inputs" or "controls" to the motion model. Exteroceptive sensors usually support measurement updates. Examples include cameras, lidar, radar, sonar, GPS, magnetometers, star trackers, and landmark detectors. They observe something outside the vehicle.

This distinction is useful because proprioceptive and exteroceptive errors have different behavior. Neither of these sensors is perfect and both categories have some degree of noise in them. Proprioceptive errors often integrate over time and create drift. Exteroceptive errors often depend on visibility, geometry, correspondence, and the map. Because of this, a navigation system that relies on only one of these two categories will eventually drift away from the truth. A good navigation system uses both to cover the other's weakness.
